overview: Two categories of homologous genes distinguished by whether they arose through speciation or gene duplication.
genZNote: Orthologs: same gene, different species, still doing its original job. Paralogs: same species, gene copied itself and went rogue.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Homologous genes in different species that arose from a single ancestral gene through a speciation event.
aspects.valueB: Homologous genes within the same genome (or across species) that arose through a gene duplication event.

aspects.label: Origin Event
aspects.valueA: Speciation — the ancestral gene diverged along with the species themselves.
aspects.valueB: Gene duplication — the ancestral gene was copied within a genome.

aspects.label: Typical Function Conservation
aspects.valueA: Usually retain the same or a very similar function across species.
aspects.valueB: Often diverge in function over time, sometimes acquiring entirely new roles (neofunctionalization).

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Human and mouse hemoglobin beta genes — same function, different species, common ancestor.
aspects.valueB: Human alpha-globin and beta-globin genes — arose from a common ancestral globin gene by duplication within the human lineage.

aspects.label: Use in Comparative Genomics
aspects.valueA: Used to infer functional conservation and study species evolution.
aspects.valueB: Used to study gene family expansion and the evolution of new functions.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Arise via speciation; found in different species.
aspects.valueB: Arise via gene duplication; can be found within the same genome.
